"Immovable stillness is simply immovable wisdom; immovable wisdom is simply immovable stillness.
Because they are of the same essence, this [identity] is applied to the particulars; therefore, there is no duality between them.

9. Question: The beginning of the *Anxin* (Settling the Mind) states: "One simply believes in the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and does not believe in its various manifestations. Does this mean that there is only the dharma-nature and no further manifestations?

If these manifestations were entirely non-existent, they would contradict what is currently perceived; furthermore, it is said that the dharma-nature is replete with all dharmas. How is this to be understood?

Answer: Because sentient beings have for many kalpas been attached only to various phenomena (*dharma*) and have not believed in the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), this teaching is expounded as an antidote to dismantle their former attachments.
It causes them to perceive only the dharma-nature within all phenomena. If one perceives the dharma-nature, one sees that the dharma-nature is entirely comprised of these very phenomena.
This dharma-nature is fundamentally without name; it is only through the provisional establishment of refuting and affirming that it is designated by the names "nature" and "phenomenon."
10. Question: All texts state that matter and mind are non-dual. If one wishes to observe this, how should one establish the contemplation?
Answer: Mind and matter are of one substance, without before or after; they are both entirely the Dharma-realm.
The sequence for cultivating contemplation must first begin with the internal mind.

If the internal mind is pure, then by means of this pure mind, one will spontaneously and effortlessly accord with all phenomena. Furthermore, one must first realize that the myriad phenomena are but mind;
only then can one contemplate the mind and thereby comprehend all phenomena. Thus, one sees that all phenomena are but mind and but form.
One should know that all things arise from the conceptualization of the mind; how could phenomena ever claim to be identical or different of their own accord?
Thus, the *Sūtra on the Examination of the Ground* states: "There are two kinds of contemplation: first, consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*); second, the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
Contemplation of the ultimate reality investigates principle, while consciousness-only examines phenomena."
When the path of contemplation on the non-duality of phenomena and principle has slightly opened, one who can understand this may be discussed regarding the Way.
(11) Question: In the *Anxin lun* (Treatise on Settling the Mind), it says: "In its essence, reality does not arise; the extinction of deluded conceptualization is called arising and ceasing.

Does this mean that one should merely eliminate deluded conceptualization while still maintaining arising and ceasing as the essence? Or does the elimination of deluded conceptualization result in the absence of arising and ceasing?

Answer: This, too, has no distinction; one must understand its underlying meaning. If discussed solely from the perspective of principle (*li*), it is neither arising nor nature. If considered in terms of the merit of the fruition, then nature does not obstruct arising.
If considered in relation to sentient beings, they possess only the arising of delusion regarding their nature. If a sage observes an ordinary person, what arises is precisely nature itself.
Here, we speak from the standpoint of returning from delusion to awakening, so as to cause one to leave arising behind and return to nature, seeing that which is neither arising nor nature.
Furthermore, fearing that those who are deluded might abandon their arising [of practice] while seeking the nature, it is taught that the essence arises, yet in reality it does not arise.
Since its arising is non-arising, its cessation is likewise non-cessation.
(12) Question: If it is said that there is only one mind of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, why may sixty-four cycles be further established? Answer: Sixty...

Regarding the fourfold [classification]: in terms of the faculties (*indriya*) and practices (*caryā*), they revolve and mutually support one another. While it is said that there are sixty-four practices when discussed comprehensively and universally, why must all these numbers be fully possessed?
Furthermore, regarding their essential nature (*svabhāva*), they simply consist in the capacity for functional application based on the quiescent illumination of the *dharmatā*.
Therefore, it is permitted to speak of them as such.

13. Question: Within this very text, it is sometimes said that "all phenomena are themselves the dharma-nature," while at other times it is said that one should investigate through the four movements and the four natures.
Which of these is the essential point?

Answer: Now, the method of contemplating the mind has both a phenomenal aspect (*dharma*) and a noumenal aspect (*tattva*). From the perspective of the noumenon, one penetrates only the Dharma-nature and proceeds no further.

From the perspective of phenomena, one focuses exclusively on observing that the four characteristics of the arising mind cannot be apprehended. This is also called "the fundamental and the derivative" (*mūla-vyavasthāna*); as the fundamental and the derivative reflect one another, phenomena and noumenon are non-dual.

14. Question: Regarding the "Contemplative Wisdom that Illuminates the Realm" in the *Fahua xuanyi*, although authentic scriptural citations have been adduced, the underlying principle remains difficult to clarify.
Answer: If one follows the teachings of the provisional expedients (*upāya*), the principle cannot be fully realized.
If explained from the ultimate perspective, the principle is easily reconciled: taking the mind as the object, the mind is also able to illumine it;
both subject and object are mind, and the essence of mind is all-pervasive. That each mind illumines every other mind is a principle that is extremely clear.
Therefore, regarding the initial statement on the inconceivable realm: the inconceivable realm is itself contemplation.
Because of this, it can be analyzed through four propositions:
the realm illuminates the realm; the realm illuminates wisdom; wisdom illuminates the realm; and wisdom illuminates wisdom.
If that which illuminates were only illumination, it could not be exhausted by description; if that which illuminates were to be described, it would not be understood through illumination.
If that which describes were only description, it could not be exhausted by illumination; if that which describes were to illuminate, it would not be understood through description.

Therefore, it is not the same as taking the insentient realm (*jaḍa-viṣaya*) to be that which is illuminated; nor is it the same as taking the deluded mind of the partial and limited [vehicles] to be that which is illuminated;
nor is it the same as taking the conventionally established *tathatā* (suchness) to be that which is illuminated.
Since that which is illuminated is thus, so too is that which illuminates; one must not treat this matter with superficiality.
15. Question: In the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (*Pó fǎ biàn*), it is stated that one must first take non-arising (*anutpāda*) as the primary principle.

Later, in the "Discrimination of the Gates," why does it further state that non-arising is wisdom (*jñāna*) and non-extinction (*anirodha*) is abandonment (*prahāṇa*)? If wisdom is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), then abandonment must be tranquility (*śamatha*). How is this so?
One should enter the gate of non-arising and contemplate only non-ceasing.

Answer: The intent of the "Gate of Universal Destruction" is to speak of partiality based on the phenomena [it addresses]. Therefore, the text states: "The wisdom of meditative concentration brings about complete purification.
This is explained in detail, as fully set forth in the commentary (*ji*).
16. Question: In the "Contemplation of the Inconceivable Realm" at the beginning of the first of the twelve contemplations on the causal conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it says:

"Unlike worldly people who grasp at attachment, a single thought-moment can encompass the three thousand [realms]. Is this the case only within this specific context, or do all realms likewise possess this quality?
Answer: All are thus. Seventeen. Question:
If that is so, one should grasp and cling to the mind as being incomplete by three thousand.
Answer: This is stated according to the application of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) regarding the object of observation.

The mind of grasping is itself the nature of all phenomena. Illuminating this grasping mind reveals it to be a dependent origination of the false and provisional. Within this provisionality, the three thousand realms are empty in their own essence;
this is precisely the inconceivable, perfect, and wondrous Three Truths of the mind-nature.
It is like a flower in the sky. The flower and the essence of space are neither one nor different. This space does not correspond to the flower or to [another] space;
it is spoken of as "empty" only in relation to the flower, yet in its own nature, it is nameless.
By this subtle analysis, one may infer that all phenomena are likewise so.
(18) Question: In the passage concerning the wondrous realm of the twelve links of dependent origination, they are grouped into three paths to correspond with the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Since the body of suffering is obstructed by its substantial nature, how can it correspond to the *dharmakāya*?
Answer: This is explained according to principle. It is stated this way by taking the body as a counterpart to the body for the sake of clear contrast.

In reality, the three bodies have no sequence of before or after. Furthermore, we discuss the beginningless wheel of suffering which is boundless; it is neither identical to nor separate from karma and afflictions.
Moreover, in the present text, the causes and conditions are discussed in terms of a single thought-moment across the ten realms and hundred realms. Based on these causes...
Based on this, one discusses the three paths; by means of these three paths, one discusses the three virtues. Therefore, the three paths and the three virtues have no sequence of before or after.
The three causes of the nature-virtue (xingde) are never absent at any time; how could one further inquire about their obstruction or impediment?
19. Question: Someone has asked: "In this land, the authentic transmission of the Dharma has followed a continuous lineage. Although the curricula have expanded, the original flavor remains intact;
by seeking the source of the school, one can naturally realize the fundamental principle. Why, then, must you further establish 'one mind' and 'three contemplations'?
To subject these to the scrutiny of the 'four movements' is merely to muddy my clear stream."
Answer: A deep current is originally clear; it becomes turbid only when disturbed.

The essence of the true source is pure; how could its being mixed hinder it? Even if a sage from India were to arrive, it would not compare to the descent of one who has two more births remaining in Tuṣita.
Therefore, even the Great Master of Dongyang, whose rank was that of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-sambodhi), still took the three contemplations and four movements as the core of his practice.
Thus, his "Poem on Solitude" says: "Solitude is refined; in truth, it transcends names and sounds. Through the three contemplations within a single mind, the myriad things are harmonized."
Where do the thickets of thorns grow?
I act alone. I ask: what is it that my mind clings to? Examining the four phases of time, nothing arises. How could a thousand ends and ten thousand entanglements bind me?
How much more so for the *Sūtra of the Necklace*, which is the fundamental source of the Three Contemplations;
it was personally received from the golden mouth of a Great Being on the verge of Buddhahood.

Thus we know that the teaching tradition of this single school (the Tiantai) received its distant transmission from the Buddha’s scriptures, and furthermore, it accords with those Great Beings as perfectly as two halves of a tally.

Moreover, as for the principles employed herein: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* serves as the core essence; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* serves as the guiding compass; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* serves as the supporting branches;
and the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* serves as the method of contemplation. Various sūtras are cited to augment faith, and various śāstras are cited to assist in its accomplishment.
Contemplating the mind is the warp; all phenomena are the woof. Woven together, they form a complete volume that is unlike any other.
Question: The Master’s oral instructions were intended solely for treating illness; are there not further essential points of mind?
Answer: All [these verses] treat illnesses.
There is only one verse which says: "The Master once taught and admonished: 'With a real mind, bind to a real object; through real conditions, they arise in succession.'"
"Reality and reality mutually infuse one another; naturally, one enters the principle of reality. The commentary states:
If the mind is bound to an object, the object is necessarily bound to the mind. This mutual binding of mind and object is called "real conditioning" (*bhūtapratyaya*).

Furthermore, because subsequent moments of mind continue in succession, this mutual binding of moment-to-moment minds is called "mutual infusion. This is precisely the mind infusing itself into the object.
The object is focused upon the object; the object is focused upon the mind; the mind and the mental objects are focused upon one another moment by moment.

In this sequence, without any interval between moments, one naturally enters the stage of partial realization through a semblance of contemplative practice. Therefore, it is said that one "enters the reality."
Regarding the sixth point, the illustration of how the aspects of practice and understanding mutually support one another:
as in the "Analysis" section, ten general meanings are used to analyze ten chapters. Within this, for the time being, we shall focus on self-cultivation and the transformation of others.

Thus, of the preceding eight [factors], the first seven are self-practice. Within these, when discussing the cause in relation to the fruit, the fruit of retribution is taken as the "fruit," which is not the primary intention here.

The first seven serve as the causes, clearly elucidating the characteristics of cultivation. Among these seven causes, the first five give rise to understanding (*adhimukti*), while the latter two constitute practice (*caryā*).

Although in the analysis of the text the "arising of the teaching" is used as a metaphor for one's own [practice], the meaning of "arising the teaching to transform others" corresponds to "understanding" (解).
This is because taking up the text out of sequence involves transforming others. Therefore, regarding the understanding of one's own practice, only the first five chapters are so designated.
Although the general meaning includes passages concerning practice, retribution, and so forth, these merely demonstrate practice, retribution, and the like to make known the beginning and end;
they do not mean that these are themselves the characteristics of cultivation.

What is this? In practice, all must take twenty-five dharmas as the preparatory means (*upāya*), and the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) and ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) as the primary cultivation. Why is this so?
If there were no ten vehicles, there would be no substance; if there were no ten dharmas, it would be like a "ruined donkey-cart."
Thus, one should know that it is necessary to rely on all five chapters to give rise to profound understanding.

Within the process of generating this understanding, the general meaning provides a concise explanation of the beginning and end, while the causes and effects of self and others are presented with brief wording but expansive significance. The subsequent four chapters focus exclusively on names and essences, wherein both the literary expression and the underlying principles are extensive.
Therefore, one employs extensive exegesis to guide the commencement of practice, causing the twenty-five dharmas to be distinguished according to the teachings;
only when the coarse elements are integrated, opened up, and discarded can it be called the beginning of wondrous practice.

Therefore, these five chapters must not be discarded as one. If one practices the ten dharmas using this interpretation, then merely explaining the names of the ten dharmas and their sequential order is sufficient for the principle.
However, the characteristics are still explained extensively in the current text because those of dull faculties might otherwise fail to understand the sequence of the contemplative methods;
thus, the previous interpretation is cited and discussed in detail for the sake of entering contemplation. Furthermore, there is concern that [the text] might become overly prolix.

The text therefore provides a comprehensive explanation of the ten dharmas within the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas). Nine of these objects are to be known through inference; thus, throughout the various passages, there is nothing that is not either secondary or primary.
For instance, the ten objects are merely the ground upon which a single moment of mind operates; each one is displayed as having distinct characteristics.
Each [stage] arises from the ten modes of contemplation; this is the seed of practice. Each transforms into the inconceivable realm; this is the sprout of practice.
Each gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; this is the trunk of practice. Each brings about the settling of the mind; this is the leaf of practice.

Each successive stage—from the thorough breaking down [of attachments] up to the primary and auxiliary practices—is the flower of the path. Each successive rank and position, culminating in the departure from craving, is the fruit of the path.
Without these six matters, the tree of the Way will not stand upright.
Although the sequence is thus, if one speaks from the perspective of human capacity, those of superior faculties produce the fruit directly from the seeds within the object;
therefore, the text says that upon merely hearing these words, the illness is immediately cured. For those of middling and inferior faculties, further subsequent methods are required;
hence the text says that they went to the elder’s place to have various medicines compounded.

Furthermore, regarding the ten vehicles, one must further understand the textual intent of each one. Each is based upon inconceivable *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and clear observation), which is the marrow of the text.
The sequential order of the arising of the characteristics of each vehicle is the bone of the text.

The various cited examples that assist in establishing the aspects of practice are the flesh of the text. The extensive refutations of ancient [views] and the resolution of doubts through question and answer are the... [of the text].
This refers to the skin.
Furthermore, according to the four texts such as the *Shiming*, the meaning of "skin" (*fū*) encompasses both the sense of skin and the sense of flesh; it is precisely the bone.
The destination reached beneath the bone is the marrow (*zhuì*).
If these four matters are absent, the Dharma-body will not be realized.

Therefore, readers and practitioners must understand what is urgent and what is secondary; they must not err in their indications, nor speak with partiality or biased intent, thereby causing the practice to be incomplete.

The course of spiritual practice does not exceed the accumulation of understanding and the arousal of skillful means. One practices the cause to attain the fruit; when the fruit is fulfilled, one instructs others.
When the capacities of others meet my response, the cycle of stimulus and response ceases, and self and other alike return to the true nature of the principle of extinction.
The intention of this present school is precisely as such. Therefore, these ten chapters encompass everything without exception.
○ Regarding the seventh section, the analogy for dispelling doubts and revealing the correct doctrine:

those who study this school all receive its teachings from a single master; its principles and texts have been transmitted in succession, and ultimately there is no divergent interpretation. Yet, one might suddenly encounter a biased person...
Because he answered differently from what was asked, the matter could not be left as it was, and so he was pressed for an illustration.
He asked: "How many types of the Sudden Teaching are there?
He replied: "There are the Gradual-Sudden and the Sudden-Sudden."
The analogy states: Regarding the method of exegesis, one must first examine the original text. When the original text establishes a name, one must not seek to interpret it differently.

Even when seeking a divergent interpretation through commentary, one must still maintain that its essence remains the same. The term "sudden-sudden" (dùn-dùn) does not appear in the sutras or śāstras; it is absent from all other schools' writings except for those of our own tradition.

If both the name and the essence were non-existent, upon what could one rely in the practice of cultivation? If one takes "sudden-sudden" to be identical to the Perfect (yuán), as in the Perfect [Teaching]...

[The opponent says: "The meaning of 'perfect' (*yuan*) and so forth may be acceptable. Since you have already divided [the teachings] into two—sudden and gradual—and designated the gradual-sudden as 'perfect,' for what purpose is the 'sudden-sudden' added?
Question: What is the difference between these two stages in terms of severing delusions?"
Answer: The two positions differ. For those who progress gradually or through sudden enlightenment, the four abodes (*catur-vihāra*) are eliminated prior to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

For those who attain sudden-sudden enlightenment, they fully subdue the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*) prior to the first stage, and from the time they ascend to the stages onward, they completely shatter the five abodes.
The analogy states: "The four abodes prior to the first abode are eliminated first. This citation belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), and this is the case throughout;
therefore, the *Perfect Teaching’s Four Mindfulnesses* says: "It is like smelting iron to make a vessel; the primary aim is to complete the vessel, not merely to remove impurities.

The coarse impurities are removed first, which does not pertain to gradual succession. Since it is said that one 'ascends to the abodes' through sudden and total penetration, this clearly indicates that the five abodes prior to the [first] abode are eliminated."

It is entirely present. One should know that this meaning is neither distinct nor exclusively perfect. If it were exclusively perfect, then the first stage (*bhūmi*) would only destroy ignorance (*avidyā*);

it would not be the case that upon entering the stages, all five dwellings (*nivāsa*) are severed simultaneously. If it were distinct, then the four dwellings would have to be fully present prior to the stages, with the dwelling-stage destroying the four dwellings, the practice-stage (*caryā-bhūmi*) destroying the *rajas-reṇu* (dust-like afflictions), and only upon ascending to the ground-stage (*bhūmi-bhūmi*) would one destroy a single grade of ignorance.
Therefore, we know it is not distinct; for apart from these two, there is no separate teaching established upon which to rely.
Question: Regarding the two types of simultaneous cultivation, what is the distinction between their characteristics?

Answer: For one who practices gradual and simultaneous contemplation, the contemplation of emptiness is established first; for one who practices sudden and sudden contemplation, all three contemplations are realized simultaneously.

The analogy states: This greatly contradicts the scriptural texts of our own school. Since it is said that "gradual perfection" refers to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) among the four teachings, one should judge this stage of perfection according to the six levels of identity (*liujie*).
Thus, one should not say that the contemplation of emptiness is first accomplished. Why?

Because the five grades correspond to the three contemplations of the stage of practice through contemplation (*guanxing*), the six faculties correspond to the three contemplations of the stage of semblance (*xiangsi*), and from the first abode (*chuzhu*) onward corresponds to the three contemplations of partial realization (*fenzheng*).

Regarding "contemplation": why do you say that the contemplation of emptiness is first accomplished? Furthermore, you fail to understand the meaning of the statement that the falling away of the views and afflictions occurs prior to the stage of semblance (*sadr̥śa-bhūmi*).

If it were already accomplished beforehand, how could it be called the "stage of semblance"? Since it is said that all three contemplations are simultaneously realized in the "sudden-sudden" [approach], what stage does this correspond to?
If it were in the first *vihāra* (abode), how would it differ from the gradual-sudden approach? If it were prior to the *vihāras*, there is no such principle at all. If you say...

Prior to the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is only suppression; at the first stage, both [suppression and abandonment] occur simultaneously. To claim otherwise would constitute a heterodox teaching, as there is no textual authority for it in any of the various scriptures.
Question: On what basis can we know that there are two kinds of suddenness?

Answer: According to the *Xuánwén*, the eight teachings consist of the gradual (*jiàn*), the sudden (*dùn*), the secret (*mìmì*), and the indeterminate (*bùdìng*). The gradual teaching is further divided into four:
the *zàng*, *tōng*, *bié*, and *yuán*. These four, together with the preceding [three], constitute the eight teachings.

Since the final *yuán* is already included within the gradual, yet a separate "sudden" is established outside of the gradual, we know that the former *yuán* is merely the gradual *yuán*, while the separately established "sudden" is indeed the true sudden teaching.
Sudden [Enlightenment] repeatedly used this argument to challenge others; no one could respond, and he alone claimed to know it.
The analogy says: according to this judgment, there are many contradictions.

First is the hindrance of failing to recognize the name of the teaching. To establish a separate "Sudden" [teaching] as a distinct category is precisely because the *Avataṃsaka* is the initial Sudden section.

When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he had not yet traveled through the various assemblies; rather than coming from the gradual, he spoke directly of the Great [Vehicle]. Because this great section stands at the beginning, it is called "Sudden.

Yet, since this section still incorporates other elements, it cannot be given the name "Sublime" (*miao*). How could one then take a scripture that incorporates other elements and translate it [as the sole Sudden teaching]?
"Each and every meal. The *Lotus Sūtra* alone reveals [the ultimate truth], yet it is termed "gradual and perfect.

These two points fail to recognize the obstacles inherent in gradual opening. Regarding what is called "gradual opening," according to the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra), after the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, a separate teaching was established for those of lesser capacity;
without moving or descending, the gradual teaching was bestowed. At the beginning of this gradual teaching, the Three Piṭakas were first expounded.
After the teaching of the Tripiṭaka, one must critique and refine it before its utility is fully realized; thus, it is said that [the latter teachings] "open up" [the former].

Therefore, in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), everything from the Deer Park assembly up to the Prajñā assemblies is termed "gradual. How could there be a Perfect Teaching within this gradual category such that it would be called "gradual-perfect"?
Furthermore, in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuán*, the classification of teachings into gradual and sudden covers the period from the *Avataṃsaka* up to the Prajñā assemblies.

All [teachings] possess both gradual and sudden aspects. Since the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) of the *Avataṃsaka* is not different from the Perfect [teachings] within the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā, they should likewise be called "Sudden-Sudden.

Why should this apply to the *Avataṃsaka* alone? If the Perfect [teachings] within the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā are termed "Gradual-Perfect," then the Perfect Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* would also be termed "Gradual-Sudden. What does this have to do with other sections?
Third is the hindrance of not recognizing the essence of the teaching (*śāsana*). If one gradually unfolds [the seven] into four, it is like opening a fist to reveal the fingers;

there is only the fingers, no fist. If one combines the four to form the gradual, it is like closing the fingers to form a fist; there is only the fist, no fingers. If the gradual is preserved, the teaching has only four;
if the gradual is subsumed, the teaching has only seven. If both are preserved, one side must lack its essence. To establish eight, however, the essence is...

Fourth is the suppression of obstacles to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In recent times, most systems of doctrinal classification (*panjiao*) have regarded the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as the primary wheel of the Dharma (*mūla-dharmacakra*) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as a secondary or derivative wheel.
Only the Great Master Tiantai, who personally received the transmission on Vulture Peak and attained great awakening at Mount Suzhou...

Master Miaowu composed his own commentaries (*zhāngshù*), comparing [the teachings] according to ten principles. He maintained that even the Trace Gate (*jìmén*) is already distinct [from the sudden], while the Source Gate (*běnmén*) is forever different.
Thus, in the *Xuánwén*, whenever there is an explanation, he first judges them by way of the teaching (*jiào*), wherein three are coarse and one is wondrous;

next, he judges them by way of the flavor (*wèi*), wherein four are coarse and one is wondrous. How can that which is coarse be called "sudden-sudden," and how can that which is wondrous be translated as "gradual-perfect"?
Fifth is the failure to recognize the obstacle posed by the name "Sudden" (dùn). If the name is established based on the practice (*xing*), then "Perfect" (*yuán*) is simply "Sudden.

For this reason, the old title was *Yuándùn Zhǐguān* (Perfect-Sudden Calm and Contemplation). If the designation is established based on the flavor (*wei*), then "Sudden" differs from "Perfect"; thus, the initial flavor is judged as "the Sudden teaching of the High Mountain.

If one were to use the "Sudden" that is associated with the flavors to critique the "Perfect" that is uniquely revealed in the classification of teachings (*panjiao*), [it would be a misunderstanding].
How mistaken! How mistaken! Sixth is the obstacle of contradicting and rejecting one's own school:
the Founder praised it as uniquely sublime, yet students disparage it as merely gradual and incomplete.
Furthermore, what benefit is there in suppressing the real and exalting the provisional?

Seventh is the obstacle of contravening the text and背离ing the meaning. The Sūtra says: "That which has been taught, that which is being taught, and that which is yet to be taught. Among these, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the foremost.

Those from the *Avataṃsaka* up to the *Prajñāpāramitā* are termed "that which has been taught"; the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (or *Anantārtha-sūtra*) is termed "that which is being taught"; and the *Mahā*... [text truncated]
The *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra* is what should be discussed by name. According to its own judgment, it has already established itself as the foremost; what does this have to do with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?
Those who hear such words spoken in private only cover their ears.
Question: If one opens up the four [teachings] from the gradual [one], and adds the previous single [gradual teaching], how do they constitute eight teachings?
Answer: After opening up the four, there remains one further gradual [teaching].

To illustrate: as was already evident from the third objection above, it is clear that [the opponent] has fallen into error; for he does not realize that the gradual [teaching] originated at the Deer Park.
Up until the *Prajñāpāramitā*, why would one separately establish a "gradual teaching"?

If one understands that from the Deer Park to the arrival of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is called "gradual" in terms of time, one will never arbitrarily judge the "Perfect" (*yuan*) within the four teachings to be a "gradual-perfect.
How could one then judge the *Lotus Sūtra* to be inferior to the "milk" teaching?
Question: As for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, what kind of "sudden" (dun) teaching is it?
It is known not to be the "sudden of the sudden.
The analogy says: This master not only fails to recognize the names "sudden" and "gradual," but he also does not understand the intent of the concluding text.

The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) concludes its explanation of the preceding four flavors of teaching. It then proceeds to conclude its explanation of the *Lotus Sūtra* by means of terms such as "gradual" and so forth, stating that it is neither sudden, gradual, secret, nor indeterminate.
Initially, it states: "Now, this *Lotus Sūtra* is manifest (*xiǎnlù*) and not secret; it is determinate (*dìng*) and not indeterminate."

The conclusion regarding the non-secret and indeterminate [teachings] does not apply [to this case]; the secret and indeterminate [teachings] encompass the preceding four periods. Next, it is stated that these are gradual and sudden, yet not gradual-gradual;
the conclusion thus excludes the teaching of "sudden first and gradual later."
Regarding the terms "gradual" and "sudden": with respect to the preceding four periods, there is the sudden within the gradual and the gradual within the sudden.

The present *Lotus Sūtra*, in its teaching of the Perfect [Truth] through the Trace Gate, does not differ in meaning from these gradual and sudden approaches; it differs only from the gradual-within-the-gradual.
Regarding the term "gradual" (*jiàn*): there is one [stage] in the Deer Park, three in the Vaipulya, and two in the Prajñāpāramitā.
The gradual within the sudden is precisely the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*); its meaning is no different from the gradual within the gradual.

Therefore, it is unnecessary to distinguish the sudden-within-sudden, as it is identical to the sudden-within-gradual, which is likewise identical to the Lotus Sūtra. For this reason, the sudden teaching need not be separately distinguished.

Therefore, in the latter part of the *Xuán* (Profound Commentary), it is stated that the "Trace Gate" (*jìmén*) of the present *Lotus Sūtra* shares both similarities and differences with other sūtras, whereas its "Root Gate" (*běnmén*) differs from all other sūtras in every respect.

What is meant by "similar" is that within various sections [of the Buddha's teachings], there is the Perfect Teaching (*yuán*). What is meant by "different" is that within various sections, there are also the three provisional teachings (*sānjiào*).

Failing to perceive this intent, you interpret the meaning based solely on the literal sound of the words and thus claim that the *Lotus Sūtra* is merely gradual-cum-sudden rather than sudden-cum-sudden.
The text simply states that it is "not gradual-gradual"; where does it ever say that it is not "sudden-sudden"?
Question: Furthermore, how is it known that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is gradual-sudden, while the *Avataṃsaka* is sudden-sudden?

Answer: According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the various śrāvakas who have come from the stage of the Small Vehicle pass through the various flavors (*rasa*) until they reach the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where they only then begin to realize the sudden teaching.
Therefore, we know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is gradual-sudden. The *Avataṃsaka* stands at the very beginning and does not pass through the various [stages].
[Because it possesses] flavor, it is thus "sudden within the sudden.
The analogy says: Now, the Lotus Sūtra is perfectly complete and fully sudden; this is based on the Dharma and not on the person.
One should not judge the sūtra as gradual simply because the śrāvakas came from the gradual [path], nor should one categorize the sūtra as gradual based solely on the śrāvakas.
Moreover, as for the śrāvakas, they do not exceed five hundred, one thousand, two thousand, or three thousand; these cases merely represent the "opening of the provisional to reveal the real.

Furthermore, there is the opening and revealing by bodhisattvas—why should it apply to śrāvakas alone? As it is said: "When bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed," and so forth.

Furthermore, the text below states: "Countless sons of the Buddha, having heard the World-Honored One’s detailed explanation, were filled with great joy throughout their bodies upon attaining the benefit of the Dharma.

It also clarifies the fundamental *tathatā* (suchness) within the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," noting those who have first resolved to attain *bodhicitta*, numbering as many as the atoms in three thousand worlds, up to the atoms in a single four-continent world, and even those in eight worlds—how much more so for those in the lower directions.
The Manifestation of the Buddha and the Wondrous Sound Sūtra came from the East. King Śubhavyūha and his retinue were converted by Mañjuśrī.
Since such multitudes as these had never before experienced the four flavors [of the Dharma], one should judge this scripture from this perspective as being "sudden within the sudden."

How much more so for the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," which states that whether in the present or after my parinirvāṇa, anyone who hears even a single phrase shall all be granted the prediction of Buddhahood.
Although the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* does not travel through the gradual stages, it cannot surpass the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for two reasons: first, its partiality;

second, its concealment of the fundamental. How could that which lacks these two meanings be called the "sudden of the sudden"? And how could that which possesses both meanings be called the "gradual"?
Question: There are also bodhisattvas who hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* all at once; why then is it judged solely from the perspective of the śrāvakas?
Answer: This is stated according to the majority of cases.
To use an analogy as previously cited: one should consider the eight elements (*dhātu*) and the hearing of a single phrase as the majority, yet conversely, [the text] uses the śrāvaka...
Regarding those who have heard much: it is not only that they do not comprehend the profound principle, but also that their reading of the text has not yet become proficient.

One should know that for śrāvakas of dull faculties and bodhisattvas whose karmic conditions had not yet matured prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they were incapable of hearing the sudden teaching.
Furthermore, by means of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings, they are further refined and prepared; only then are they capable of coming to the Lotus Sūtra to hear the sudden teaching.
Therefore, this Lotus Sūtra should be judged as "opening the gradual" and "revealing the sudden," and is thus termed "gradual-sudden."
People do not see this and claim it is not the "sudden-sudden" [teaching]. Question:
On what basis can one know that in the "gradual-round" teaching, the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*) fall away first?

Answer: It is as cited from the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Ratnarāśi-sūtra*), which speaks of a "long-term departure from the wheel of suffering. Since it mentions a "departure from suffering," we know this refers to the gradual-sudden. As cited from the *Dharmapada*... [text truncated]
The "Flower" [Sutra] speaks of the purification of the six sense organs, mentioning the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) and so forth;
this should be understood as the sudden-within-the-sudden. The analogy states: according to the doctrine of this school, both the *Renwang* and the *Fahua* are cited to corroborate one another.

The *Fahua* speaks of the "outflow-free mind-organ" (*anāsrava-mano-indriya*), while the *Renwang* speaks of "permanently departing from the three realms. Both sutras refer to the prior falling away of the four abidings (*catur-vāsana*). Furthermore, regarding...

Within the realm [of saṃsāra], one attains the name "untainted" (anāsrava) because tainted karma has been eliminated; thus it is said that they are "permanently separated. One should know that the textual meaning of these two passages is fundamentally the same.
How can they be divided and used as proof for two distinct types of simultaneous realization?
Question: Among the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, what constitutes the "sudden" aspect of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuántùn*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*?
Answer: It is the "gradual-sudden" (*jiàndùn*). How is this known? For instance, in the first fascicle, three metaphors are used for the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*;

therein, the metaphor of a practitioner soaring through the air represents the Perfect and Sudden. Furthermore, in the seventh fascicle, within the section on "Recognizing Penetration and Obstruction," it states that the Middle [Way] is the threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

It refutes the [conventional] *abhijñā* (supernormal powers). Because these *abhijñās* are refuted, they are not "sudden-sudden. The text states: "Specifically, it briefly points to three gates; the general intent lies in the 'one sudden' (*ekakṣaṇika-sadyas*).
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it says: "Now, relying on the sūtras, I shall further clarify the Perfect Sudden (*paripūrṇa-sadyas*).

Moreover, at the end of the section on settling the mind (*citta-pratiṣṭhāpana*) in the fifth fascicle, it first summarizes the number of categories based on the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and subsequently summarizes them again based on the single-mind (*ekacitta*) *śamatha*.

Regarding the enumeration of the "knots" (concluding statements): furthermore, in the first "knot" concerning the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), there are first three "knots" of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, followed by the statement, "Furthermore, it is also concluded with one *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
All such instances are the primary texts for a distinct, separate, and sudden [teaching] outside of the three [standard] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The commentary states: At first glance, citing these proofs may seem to provide some basis; yet, upon careful investigation, they are found to have no foundation whatsoever.
Why is this? Because they contradict the text and because they give rise to many difficulties.

Why is this? As was demonstrated in the refutation of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and further clarified according to the sūtras—the text of which is found in the Preface—this Preface was composed by Zhiyi (Zhang’an).
At the time when the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* was being taught, this Preface did not yet exist. How could the main body of the text have anticipated it to refute [the opponent's position]?
Furthermore, Sanlun’s own biography records that he was a disciple of Nanyue. How could a disciple then go so far as to subvert his master’s school?

This would constitute a *lōkāyata* treatise of perverse argumentation. Moreover, since Nanyue inherited the teachings from Huiven and Nāgārjuna, if [Sanlun] were to break his master’s dharma, why would he need to state in the *Guansin lun* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind) that he takes refuge in the ancestral masters?
Moreover, the two instances of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) have distinct meanings. In the introduction, the sudden practitioner is likened to one who treads upon emptiness.
Emptiness has no degrees of depth; rather, it is the treader who has steps and gradations. Emptiness is a metaphor for the sudden principle, while treading is a metaphor for the conduct of practice.

Although practice may involve gradual stages, it is still termed "gradual within the perfect" (*yuan-jian*); yet, since the principle has no depth or shallowness, it cannot be categorized as either partial or perfect. In the seventh fascicle, [the text uses] the divine horse...

This passage generally illustrates the three contemplations (trivipaśyanā) in their horizontal and distinct aspects. Since supernatural powers (abhijñā) belong within the category of distinct characteristics, the middle [contemplation]—which is itself the three contemplations—is used to refute the "middle" among these horizontal and distinct aspects.
How can you fail to see that the proximate text implicitly refutes the sequence of what has not yet arisen?

Next, regarding the further clarification based on the scriptural text: previously, three metaphors were used to verify the three types of texts; now, we further rely on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to verify the Perfect text.
Therefore, it is said to be "further clarified. This is the purpose for revising and finalizing the meaning of the text once again.
How can one see the single character "geng" (頓) and then establish the name "dun-dun" (頓頓) outside of the three [categories]?

If you cite the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as being the "dun-dun," then the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánzàng-lùn* (玄義) also cites the *Avataṃsaka*, the Vaipulya (*Fāngděng*), and the *Prajñāpāramitā* as all perfectly realizing the "dun.
Since the *Avataṃsaka* is not merely the "gradual perfection" (*jiàn yuán*), how could the Vaipulya and the *Prajñāpāramitā* not be the "dun-dun"?

Regarding the statement that "if one speaks of the distinctions, they are briefly indicated by three gates, while the general meaning lies in a single sudden [approach]," this refers to the text of the *Liaojian* (Discrimination), which briefly explains three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Since the brief summary and the general meaning share similar names, he asks again about their similarities and differences.
In the answer, two meanings—general and specific—are distinguished. The general meaning provides a brief indication, which is merely the broad intent.
The specific meaning is briefly shown to differ significantly from the former. Because they differ, there are briefly three types; the broad intent is contained within only one of these three.
Therefore, the text states that the gradual and indeterminate [approaches] are set aside and not discussed.
People, failing to see this, establish a "sudden-of-the-sudden" apart from the three [other types].
At the end of the section on settling the mind, it first concludes the count with the three successive contemplations, and then concludes the count with the single mind. Successively...

The meaning of "separate" (*bie*) corresponds to the partial (*bie*), while the meaning of "one mind" (*yixin*) corresponds to the perfect (*yuan*). This perfection is identical to the initial general "settling of the mind" (*anxin*), which serves as the basis for counting the stages.
Therefore, while the meaning opens into three separate categories, it subsequently returns to the original foundation to conclude with the one mind.
Failing to perceive this intention, divergent interpretations arise.

Regarding the statement that the final section on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) serves as a conclusion for the entire passage on the arousal of the bodhicitta: the general meaning of the five chapters is broad and comprehensive;

therefore, each is concluded with *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. At times, however, it is concluded by using only one of them, as in the sixfold "identity" (*liù jí*) passage, where all six sections are so concluded.
All are unified. Alternatively, they may be concluded using only the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, as at the end of the *Suizuyi* (Following One’s Own Intent) text.

At times, one employs all three—unity, three, and one—to conclude them, as cited previously. Furthermore, there are cases where the concluding text is missing, such as in the three kinds of samādhi beginning with "constant practice" (*nitya-caryā*).
Furthermore, if one employs all three [methods] together in a single binding, this is merely a matter of the difference between the general and the specific. Why?

Because regarding the first type of binding, it is said that "arousing the bodhicitta" is *vipaśyanā* (insight), while "the cessation of deviant thoughts" is *śamatha* (calm abiding). One should know that within these three types, there is none that does not involve arousing the mind and the cessation of deviant thoughts.
Moreover, the three types of bindings also possess a general meaning; because they apply universally to all three, they are such.
Therefore, I conclude this: from the beginning of the Tripitaka up to the Perfect and Sudden [teachings], all possess the gradual, the sudden, and the indeterminate.

This is fully detailed in the third section on "Partial and Complete" as well as in the tenth chapter of the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning) on the classification of teachings (*panjiao*). The four teachings are distinct, while the three types are common to all.
In this first passage, I do not enumerate each of the four teachings individually through the threefold conclusion, but rather treat them collectively by means of the four teachings as a whole.

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*): since three are paired with one, and these three are further distinct, people fail to perceive this and instead rely on the phrase "and again" (*you yi*) to establish them as separate entities. This is profoundly untenable.
Question: What are the similarities and differences between the two types of sudden stages (*tun-wei*)? Answer:
They differ prior to abiding in the stages (*zhuzhuan*), but are identical once one has ascended to the stages (*dengzhu*).

The analogy states: those who enumerate the stages must all rely upon the teachings; furthermore, regarding the establishment of stages by a single school of ancient masters, they distinguish only [the following]: [The text continues with the specific classification of stages.]
The four distinct [teachings] clearly manifest the causes and effects of the entire course of the teaching; from beginning to end, nothing exceeds these four.

In the Tripitaka (Śrāvaka) teaching, there are the four fruits and the Pratyekabuddhas after a hundred kalpas or three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. In the Shared Teaching, there is the common stage for the Three Vehicles, where the names differ but the meaning is shared.

In both the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, the fifty-two stages are established together; however, their practices vary in being leisurely or rapid, and they differ in their severance and subduing of afflictions. The Perfect [Teaching] relies upon...
The *Lotus Sūtra* further adds the five stages (*pañca-varga*). This is consistent across all the various sections used by our school;
I have never heard of a system involving two sessions (*dvi-kāla*), as has already been refuted previously.
Question: For what reason are two types of sudden [teaching] established through differentiation? Answer:
They are established as distinct based on the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*).

To illustrate: since ancient times, we have received and inherited the teachings of the One Perfect Vehicle; we have never seen two types of sudden teaching being divided according to two types of faculties. Where [is this found]?

In the text, it is simply stated that the *Avataṃsaka* accommodates both those of sharp and dull faculties: those of sharp faculties belong to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), while those of dull faculties belong to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
Alternatively, within each individual teaching, one may distinguish three grades of capacity; or, one may distinguish sharp and dull faculties based on the two modes of practice—faith and Dharma.

Thus, it is the case in every teaching and every section without exception. Upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, all enter together into the single reality (*eka-tattva*); there is no room for further opening or merging.

Those of a single capacity (ekayāna-gotra) are still called "dull" (*mṛdu*). When the provisional is concealed and the traces are hidden, there are both dull and sharp capacities, yet they are designated as "sharp.
This is because [the former] is profoundly unfathomable.

Question: Within the Vaipulya [sūtras], four gradual stages are opened within the four [vehicles]. Regarding these two sets of four, what are the similarities and differences between the Perfect [Vehicle] (*pariniṣpanna*) and the others?
Answer: "However, within the four teachings, the Perfect (yuan) is entirely gradual-perfect.
The analogy states: This master does not understand the meaning of the gradual teaching; therefore, he fails to realize that the Vaipulya (fangdeng) is merely one part of the gradual.
Claiming that the gradual teaching is distinct from the Vaipulya, he immediately replies: "It is simply that all four teachings are named [the Perfect]."
This refers to the gradual [teaching]. If one knows that there is no distinction [between them], why do you simply answer with the word "only"?

Even if the Perfect [teaching] within the four teachings prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly is all termed "gradual-perfect," and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* reveals only the single Perfect by opening up the provisional, for what reason do you still maintain the designation "gradual-perfect"?
If that were so, you would merely recognize the term "gradual" regarding the four teachings, yet fail to understand the opening and abolishing [of the provisional] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Master Dengyi, based on this, arbitrarily established the terminology of "gradual" and "sudden.
Question: What is the difference between [the gradual] and the "perfect" (yuan) within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*?
Answer: That, too, is gradual perfection.

The analogy says: If it were as you judge—that from the beginning at the Deer Park until the end at Nirvana, all was uniformly gradual and then perfected—then for what reason does the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) strenuously refute the Gāozhái school?

Even though the Gāozhái school maintains that the *Fǎhuá* is distinct from the previous teachings, and even when they cite those previous teachings to offer a general defense, [the *Xuánwén*] still refutes them.

Yet this master, having received the transmission of the Mountain Gate (Tiantai), turns out to be no better than the Gāozhái school. One should say: although the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* has four [aspects],...

The first three [teachings] are complete; although the Vaipulya (fangděng) possesses four [aspects], the three do not enter into the ultimate reality. Within the gradual teaching, the opening of the four is no different from that of the Vaipulya.
Since this is extensively taught in various texts, why should there be further doubt? According to their own arguments, the "perfect *ī*" (*yuán ī*) of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* would then become useless.
Furthermore, there is one practice that is merely a hollow pretense.
Question: Do all four teachings of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* enter into the Perfect [Teaching]?
Answer: There are those who do not; the ten classes of non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) are precisely such cases.
The analogy says: You have merely heard the words that "Nirvana enters the reality," yet you do not understand the meaning of attaining entry through gathering [the fruits].

If the ten sages did not enter the threefold cultivation, how could they have heard that there is neither beginning nor end, and thus no middle—how then could they have entered? Since the ten sages did not enter, for what reason did the World-Honored One preach permanence for them?

[The opponent] objects: "In your [Buddhist] system, although the cause is permanent, the fruit is not. [The author] refutes this, saying: "In your non-Buddhists' [system], although the cause is permanent, the fruit is not."

"Permanence! Within my Buddha-dharma, it is because the cause is impermanent that the fruit is permanent; even down to Cunda’s statement that form is permanent, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent.
The general view of all other non-Buddhists is likewise so. How can you erroneously judge this to be impermanent?"
If even the texts that are easy to perceive contain errors, how much more so those that are difficult to perceive?

Question: In the first fascicle of the *Zhiguan*, there are various metaphorical passages, such as "the voice of the kalaviṅka bird," "pounding ten thousand kinds of ingredients into a pill," "bathing in the great ocean," and "agada medicine.
For what purpose are these used as metaphors? Answer: [They serve to illustrate] suddenness.
Answer: Both are gradual and sudden. Why? Because while still within the eggshell, the myriad things must be pounded;
one must await the various waters entering the great ocean, and combine all medicines to form *agada*. Therefore, these are gradual-sudden.

If one does not emerge from the eggshell, the various waters are already the ocean, and the myriad things need not be pounded nor combined into medicine; to spontaneously possess [the result] is sudden-sudden.
The commentary states: There are two faults here. First, not understanding the intent of the analogy; second, contradicting one’s own words. Regarding the failure to understand the analogy:
generally speaking, an analogy applies only to a partial aspect. Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "True liberation cannot be illustrated by means of an analogy.
For example, when comparing a snow mountain to an elephant, how could one expect to find its tail or tusks? When using a fan as an analogy for the moon, how [could it be otherwise]?
One may seek its radiance and its suspension; how much more so the intended meaning of the original text? The intent lies in a single dharma that encompasses all dharmas.
Taking what is presently perceived as a metaphor: before entering the ocean, the waters are incomplete; before being pounded into a pill, the various essences are insufficient.
The other birds among the brood do not cry out; likewise, although other medicines may be compounded to treat diseases, they do not apply universally.

Therefore, these are used as immediate metaphors. How can you refute the metaphor and claim it is gradually perfected? To raise a child who is unworthy and then to blame others for the fault is a grievous error.
The metaphors are precisely the matters at hand.
Second, regarding the contradiction with one's own words: you yourself established the general thesis that [the teachings] are "sudden within the sudden.
Since these metaphorical texts all pertain to this general thesis, how can you now disparage them as being "gradual" and "incomplete"?
Question: In the first fascicle, it was stated that they were not actually father and son, but were both called "wayfarers. To what do these metaphors refer? Answer:
That they were not actually of the same flesh and bone refers to the two preceding teachings; that they were both called "wayfarers" refers to the two subsequent teachings.
The analogy states: This profound meaning is not apparent within the text. The text presents a principle for both the internal realm and the external realm;

each principle employs two teachings as the means of expression (*vyañjaka*), and both utilize the Four Noble Truths as the basis for delusion and liberation. These points are integrated within the text itself.

Anger is illustrated by the analogy of gathering; striking is illustrated by the analogy of suffering. If the two parties are father and son, anger and striking are slight, which is illustrated as a direct teaching.

If the two are strangers, anger and striking are severe, which is used as a metaphor for a circuitous path. This refers to the differences in the realization of the knowledge of the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).

Therefore, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is both identical to and distinct from [the Truth of Suffering and its Cause]. If they are understood as identical, then suffering and its cause are identical to the principle, like a traveler being father and son.
If they are understood as distinct, then suffering and its cause are different from the principle, like father and son being travelers.

One should know that in reality, they are not two pieces of flesh and bone called "travelers"; this is merely according to the meaning of "distinction" in the crude teaching. Furthermore, it lacks the definitive judgment regarding what is within the realms (*dhātu*).

[The opponent] says: "This is clumsy. Why then do you cross over the boundaries [of the teachings] to establish four distinct doctrines? This is explained in detail as it appears in the *Zhiguan ji* (Commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*).
Question: Are the *Jian* (Gradual) and *Bie* (Distinct) teachings the same or different?
Answer: These two are not the same. The gradual [teaching] opens up four [stages], whereas the distinct [teaching] does not open up four.
The analogy says: since you do not recognize that the gradual teaching opens up four stages, what benefit is there in merely distinguishing it from the distinct teaching?

Regarding the statement that "now, when speaking of the gradual and distinct [teachings], all should be opened into four," the two texts differ. As previously explained, the gradual teaching opens into four;

as for the distinct opening into four, it is fully detailed within the Four Great Vows of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). In summing up the realm of the Four Truths, one passes through all four teachings, yet one must thoroughly understand the reason why they are opened into four.
However, for those of the distinct teaching, this may not necessarily apply in its entirety to both their own practice (*zixing*) and their transformation of others (*huata*).

The names of the four teachings are established merely as "within the realm" and "beyond the realm," "crooked" and "straight," and "clumsy" and "skillful. As for one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*), one enters vertically through successive stages;

as for transforming others (*para-parivartana*), one reaches them horizontally according to conditions. Although the reaching of sentient beings is horizontal, the practice ultimately becomes vertical;

although one's own practice is vertical, universal study results in horizontality. For example, when first entering emptiness, if one exclusively employs either analytical or intrinsic methods to destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), this remains partial.

One practices the eight gates of self-cultivation through a single gate; when one reaches the ten practices for the sake of benefiting others, only then does one universally study the eight gates of analyzing the essence (*tattva*) as well as the immeasurable and unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) eight gates. What is practiced at that time may then be called "horizontal" (*tiryak*).
This constitutes the fulfillment of the four teachings of others.
When reading this text, if one does not grasp the meaning thoroughly and treats the principles with negligence, one will erroneously judge that the distinctions are not fourfold.
Question: To which part of the text does the phrase "a general discussion" (*shānglüè*) refer?
Answer: It refers to the passage beginning with "Drawing from the stream to seek the source."

The commentary states: This also involves two errors. First, a failure to understand the meaning of the old and new texts; second, a mistaken judgment regarding the succession of the patriarchal lineage.

Regarding the first, the failure to understand the textual meaning: the old text consists of ten chapters; the first five are the introduction (*nidāna*), and the latter five are the main body (*śarīra*). Thus, the old...

The *Benchu* (Original Preface) states: "I have privately reflected that the work shall consist of ten chapters in total. The first five, beginning with 'A Brief Discussion' (*shanglüe*), are termed 'Private Reflections' (*qienian*) because they represent my own private reflections used to introduce the sequence.
The latter five, beginning with 'Opening the Chapters' (*kaizhang*), are termed 'Accounts of What Was Heard' (*shuwen*) because they recount what I personally heard at the Dharma assembly.
As for the re-editing and revision, it was done so that 'Private Reflections' should not be directly connected to 'Accounts of What Was Heard' to form the ten chapters."
The titles of the five chapters of the *Shanglue* (Examination) were abolished. Although the chapter titles were abolished, their texts remained.

In the *Shuwen* (Account of What Was Heard), although the sequence of the five chapters remains, the chapter titles have been omitted. The text of the *Shanglue* has been newly relocated to serve as examples for corroboration.

The words "Zhi-guan" (Cessation and Contemplation) and so forth have been added at the beginning to serve as the general preface (*tongxu*), while the passage beginning with "Yiliu" (Drawing in the Stream) is used to correspond to the specific preface (*biexu*). [Person]...
Not having seen it, he speaks in confusion. He vainly attempts to reconcile the old text with the new preface by means of conjecture;
yet, alas, these conjectural writings further manifest after the lineage of the patriarchs—this is truly unacceptable.

Question: From "Drawing from the stream" (*yiliu*) onwards, the text precisely follows the lineage of the original version; how can it be considered a text for "investigative deliberation" (*shanglüe*)?
Answer: It is precisely because this section investigates whether there is a teacher or no teacher that it is called "investigative deliberation."

The Commentary states: The previous explanation of "briefly deliberating" (*shānglüè*) says it is a concise summary of the Buddhist scriptures that roughly clarifies the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]; hence it is called "briefly deliberating.
It cites passages from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* such as "comprehensively understanding" (*liǎodá*), "Wénxuánshǒu" (*Xiánshǒu*), and "hearing the Perfect" (*wén yuán*).

Now, however, these texts concerning the ancestral transmission are judged to be "briefly deliberating" regarding whether there was a teacher or no teacher. Since the ancestral transmission itself is taken as the object of "briefly deliberating," if one were to further point to the ancestral transmission...
The subsequent section clarifies the distinctions. From beginning to end, there have been repeated false explanations.

Question: Regarding these three dharmas—the mental factors of sentient beings, the form of sentient beings, and the external environment and retribution—what is the difference between observing them suddenly (*ton*) and observing them suddenly-suddenly (*ton-ton*)?
Answer: In the "Sudden-Sudden" stage of contemplation, one is immediately endowed with all dharmas; in the "Gradual-Sudden" stage, the mind is endowed [with them].
In the other two stages, there is no such endowment. The analogy states: according to this answer, the "Gradual-Round" stage is actually employed as the "Sudden-Sudden."
Why is this? Among the four teachings, the Perfect Teaching (the *yuan*) has always been said to possess the dharmas in three locations. Thus, in the passage on the perfect *smṛtyupasthāna*, it says:
"It is not only consciousness-only; there are also only form, only sound, and only touch."
The teaching that fully possesses the Dharma across the three stages is precisely the Perfect (Yuan) teaching at the conclusion of the four teachings.
To now erroneously judge this as a text of the "Sudden within the Sudden" (Dun-dun) is to be proven, by examination, to have merely used one's own subjective opinions in making such judgments.

Furthermore, once one has gradually perfected the realization that the mind possesses all phenomena and that all phenomena are universally subsumed within it, how could there be any separation from form?
Since form is subsumed within the mind and the mind is itself form, how can you erroneously judge that only the mind possesses [phenomena]?
If it were a person following the Separate Teaching (biejiao), then from the very first moment of mind, both form and mind would not yet possess the dharmas; why then speak of form alone?

The gradual and sudden teachings intermingle and alternate, making the gates of instruction complex and diverse. Since the gates of instruction are thus diverse, practicing contemplation based upon them is like wandering in the dark of night.
Question: What is the distinction between these two types of contemplation at the initial stage of the mind?

Answer: Regarding those who practice sudden-sudden contemplation, at the moment they first resolve their minds, they contemplate all three truths simultaneously. Regarding those who practice gradual-sudden contemplation, they first contemplate the Middle Way as being free from the two extremes;

once these two contemplations are first established, the afflictions of view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought-delusion (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are destroyed beforehand, and only subsequently do they realize the Middle Way, whereupon the three truths are fully realized.
The same applies here. The analogy states: although one may establish "sudden-sudden" by citing three or five locations within the text, there is no orthodox principle for doing so;

furthermore, there is no canonical text that defines stages based on contemplation (*guan*). The Great Master merely cites various sutras to clarify the stages as proof for the four teachings; he does not [do otherwise].

He cites evidence to establish a separate "Sudden" teaching outside the four teachings; yet, even those passages concerning the "Sudden" found throughout various texts are all the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* (the Perfect) at the final stage of the four teachings.
He takes this Perfect [teaching] and judges it to be the "Gradual Perfect," claiming that those who first resolve their minds first contemplate the Middle Way.
However, there is no such text in any of the teachings. Specifically, one must first contemplate the two extremes before one can see [the Middle].

If the contemplation of the afflictions (思, *vitarka*) falls first, how could it be that the Middle Way alone is observed to first destroy the views and afflictions? Thus, both the Perfect and Distinct [teachings] would lack any basis for their establishment.
Question: What is the difference between the two phrases "the three contemplations within one mind" and "one mind as the three contemplations"?

Answer: One mind and three contemplations are precisely the provisional (prajñapti). Three contemplations and one mind are precisely the empty (śūnyatā). Neither three nor one is precisely the middle (madhyama).

It is called "empty and provisional" for the purpose of destroying [the attachment to] the supernatural powers of foot-travel and horse-riding; however, if we discuss the suddenness of the sudden, the one contains the three.

The analogy states: The three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) in this fundamental treatise must have a specific purpose; these constitute the great essence of the Buddha-dharma and are the essential gateway of this school.

Whenever one employs their names, they must point to actual reality. Since these three categories are used to encompass all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), one must understand the three meanings in order to fully exhaust the scope of this gateway.
First is "forming contemplation in relation to the object," as seen in such passages as "contemplating the one mind as the inconceivable object" and "the universal shattering of dharmas.
Second is "summarizing through commentary," as in the first fascicle’s discussion of "convergence and dispersion," "neither convergence nor dispersion," and "three-in-one yet not three."
It is not that they are identical.
Third, they are established by relying on provisional names and meanings. For example: "gate" is neither gate nor non-gate, and "expedient" and "real" are neither expedient nor real, and so forth.
These three contemplations are one mind, and one mind is the three contemplations; this is entirely not the intended meaning of these three contemplations.
It is merely a reversal and refutation of that vertical and horizontal contemplation.

Since the vertical contemplation concerns only the sequential three and does not attain the one, it uses "three within the one" to refute the meaning of the vertical. Therefore, it is said that "one-mind three-contemplations" refutes the vertical and penetrates [the horizontal].
"Blockage. When viewed horizontally, one obtains only the individual parts and not the three as a whole; therefore, by means of the "one within the three," one breaks through that horizontal text.
Thus it is said: "The three contemplations within one mind break through that horizontal obstruction and blockage."
People do not see this and thus apply "double negation" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta) as an antidote to the three contemplations.
Furthermore, the text itself states: "Because emptiness is itself the three, one abandons walking on foot; because the provisional is itself the three, one abandons riding a horse;
because the middle is itself the three, one abandons supernatural powers."
That master then said: "The terms 'emptiness' and 'provisionality' are spoken in order to refute the supernatural powers of walking and horse-riding;
however, walking and horse-riding are themselves merely emptiness and mere provisionality. Why is it necessary to further refute them with emptiness and provisionality?"
This destroys the arbitrary distinction between the "step-by-step" (krama) and the "supernormal power" (ṛddhi) [approaches]. In the Perfect Teaching (yāna), the One inherently contains the Three.
Why, then, do you separately state, "If one discusses the 'sudden-of-the-sudden' (ton-ton), the One contains the Three"?

This is a textual contradiction and a fallacious explanation that causes those who rely on the text to become confused. Furthermore, it is an erroneous formulation of contemplation that causes those who practice meditation to rashly accept it.
Question: What are the similarities and differences between the relative (*sāpekṣa*) and the absolute (*anapekṣa*)?
Answer: The sudden-sudden is the absolute; the gradual-sudden is the relative.
[The opponent] says by way of analogy: "This is a grave error. According to this judgment, both the relative and the absolute should be neither sudden-sudden nor gradual-sudden."
Why is this? Because in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Commentary), it is judged that the present *Lotus Sūtra* possesses two meanings: namely, the relative (*xiāngdài*) and the absolute (*juédài*).
If that is so, where else would there be a distinct "sudden-sudden" [teaching] that is absolute?
Furthermore, according to that judgment, it would follow that only the *Avataṃsaka* is absolute (*atyanta*) while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is purely relative (*apekṣā*).

If one understands that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* possesses both meanings, and further divides the relative and absolute into two types of sudden teaching (*tun*), then one should know that such a judgment contradicts its own words.
Based on this, it can be argued that [the opponent] is confused regarding both types of relativity.

Why is this? If both [the provisional and the ultimate] must await one another, yet are not gradual but only sudden, then to judge them as "mutually dependent" (*xiāngdài*) while also judging them as "gradual" constitutes a further layer of self-contradiction in one's own words.

Generally speaking, when one speaks of mutual dependence, it means that the preceding teachings are considered gradual and coarse, whereas the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is considered sudden and subtle.
Since the sudden is situated after the gradual, it includes what was refuted; it clarifies the sudden by contrast with the gradual. Therefore, it is said:
Regarding the gradual and the sudden, people do not perceive them; they merely distinguish between "relative" (*dai*) and "absolute" (*ze*) to correspond to two sutras.
Furthermore, they do not understand the meaning of the absolute relative. That which is absolute in relation to what it depends upon—being termed "absolute relative"—is precisely the wondrous sudden.
That [position] departs from the Sudden; it establishes the "Ultimate" (jue) by waiting for the distinct. What, then, is called the "Sudden-of-the-Sudden"? Question:
This *Lotus Sūtra* fully possesses both types of waiting; how can one depart from the text to judge it as belonging to two paths?
Answer: From the very beginning, there has never been duality; it is only when they have not yet realized this that they are distinct.

The analogy is as follows: this master is not only deluded regarding the profound texts concerning the names of "provisional" (*dai*) and "ultimate" (*jue*), but he also fails to comprehend the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s "opening and convergence" (*kaie*).
Within the teachings of a single lifetime, all doctrines converge in the *Lotus Sūtra*; yet he judges the *Lotus Sūtra* to contain only the provisional.

Furthermore, what section could be established as the "Convergence Sūtra"? If one were to use the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to converge with the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, there is in fact no teaching of "opening and revealing" [the latter through the former].

If that were the case, since neither would have been converged, one should instead establish a separate sūtra to converge these two. If one attempts to converge them through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), there is no textual basis for such a convergence.

The judgment of our school is that the *Lotus Sūtra* is absolutely superior to the *Avataṃsaka*. One should know that this clearly demonstrates that the "flower-retribution" [of the *Avataṃsaka*] has not yet reached its ultimate consummation.
Furthermore, it is not merely that it is not yet consummated; it is also that it lacks independence. Because it incorporates the "Distinct" (*byō*) teaching, it cannot manifest in isolation;
since it does not even exist in relation to others, what could possibly serve as its point of reference for superiority?
When the assembly has concluded, there is no duality; they all return to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Why, then, is it judged to be "not sudden-sudden"? Question:
Are there not passages in the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that do not accord with this?
Answer: It is designated as "sudden" in contrast to what preceded it; there should be no other principle [to the contrary].
